I would also use topical magnesium chloride and consider topical DMSO with a known-genuine CBD preparation as adjuncts (a lot of CBD is fake or very dilute). Seizures come in all different types, and we have no study on whether CBD could be a rescue remedy for a seizure (just anecdotes), even though we do have studies showing long-term effectiveness to prevent them: Purified oral CBD is approved for the seizures of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex. For focal seizures outside those syndromes, the evidence is mixed, but still long-term.

And topical CBD hasn't been well-studied. There was a short 12-week trial done, where they used a CBD skin gel, and it did show that transdermal absorption works like oral CBD's but the dosing was too low, and transdermal CBD also doesn't get converted to the potentially more active form (7-OH-CBD) by the liver.

As for DMSO, it did reduce seizure activity in rats with temporal-lobe epilepsy, and we know it has several neuroprotective mechanisms, but it produced the opposite effect at some doses in an absence-epilepsy model. I'd treat it as a plausible experimental adjunct remedy rather than something to wait on while a seizure continues.

And topical CBD hasn't been well-studied. There was a short 12-week trial done, where they used a CBD skin gel, and it didn't do any better than placebo. The gel got CBD into the blood at about the levels of the starting oral dose, 5 to 10mg/kg. The approved oral doses go up to 20 or 25mg/kg a day, so the dosing may have been too low. Transdermal CBD also skips the liver's first pass, so less of it gets converted to 7-OH-CBD, a form that stopped seizures in mice about as well as CBD itself.

Some people feel a seizure coming before it takes hold, and in that warning a few things people report can still stop it for some of them, depending on what sets it off. If it's flashing or flickering light, cover one eye with a hand and turn away from the light, because closing the eyes doesn't block enough of it. Some people stop a seizure at the warning stage with a strong smell like jasmine, and some train themselves to link one smell with feeling calm and then sniff it when a seizure threatens. When overstimulation is what sets it off, a cool, quiet, dark and comfortable space can help.

Some people with epilepsy smoke or vape cannabis the moment an aura starts, and they say it keeps the seizure from going further. One woman's EEG showed fewer seizure discharges on the days she smoked. Other people say THC vapes and concentrates brought their seizures on, though. And in rats, high-THC smoke made absence seizures worse, which are the brief staring kind. It takes someone fully awake to smoke or vape safely, so this is just for the warning stage, never for someone who's already convulsing.

Anything that could let someone hurt themselves in the next five minutes takes priority, so get the car keys out of reach and turn the stove off, and move them away from roads and balconies, or pools of water for that matter. Put any weapons away and keep the person away from crowds and strangers. If they want to post their big revelation about the universe, or message an ex, take the phone.

Letting them move around is fine, and pacing can help, but keep them from taking more of anything. If they want to go confront somebody, that can wait. And if they want to leave, someone goes with them.
